idiom_name: static operator overloads on a readonly record struct (public static Money operator +(Money, Money))
implementation_notes: Overload the arithmetic operators as static members of an immutable struct or record: public static Money operator +(Money left, Money right) returns a new instance built from the canonical fields, so a + b on the type yields the type and call sites never touch primitives. What replaces the classic structure is exactly this operator declaration plus the record's value equality - the pattern needs no other machinery; validate currency and normalise the representation inside the operator (and in the constructor) so every result is a valid value. Operator form is still justified whenever combinations appear in expressions; for non-arithmetic combinations use a plainly named method, and prefer a readonly record struct so the value cannot be mutated through a reference. When generic algorithms must fold your type, add the C# 11 generic-math variant below instead of duplicating overloads.
pitfalls: Overloading + but not ==/!= (or leaving the record's synthesised equality disagreeing with a normalising +) makes two visibly equal totals compare unequal; normalise in the constructor.
Operator overloads on a mutable class with reference semantics invite aliasing: use readonly record struct so a combination cannot be observed through another reference.

There is no compile-time unit or currency check inside an operator, so a mismatch must be rejected at runtime - and the exception type should be documented, because it now surfaces from an arithmetic expression.

variants.name: Static abstract interface members (generic math)
variants.implementation_notes: From C# 11 (.NET 7) the type can declare that it is closed under + in the type system: implement IAdditionOperators<TSelf, TOther, TResult> and the identity via IAdditiveIdentity, and any generic algorithm constrained as where T : IAdditionOperators<T, T, T> can fold your type with the ordinary + operator. This is a typeclass-style realization of the same pattern - the closure is no longer just a signature convention but a constraint other code can require - and it is the reason to pick this variant when you write reusable aggregation helpers over several value types. Choose the default operator-overload variant instead when the type is only combined inside the application and no generic algorithm ever needs to know it is addable; the two compose, so a type can ship the operators and add the interfaces later.
pitfalls: The interface constraint is a promise about semantics as well as syntax: a Money that implements IAdditionOperators but throws on currency mismatch breaks generic algorithms in ways the constraint cannot express.
Static abstract members need matching static declarations; the compiler reports them as interface-implementation errors, not as missing operators, which is confusing at first.

IAdditiveIdentity requires a single neutral value, but Money carries a currency, so the identity is only meaningful per currency - constrain the interface to types where a genuine identity exists (or carry the currency elsewhere).
